## Loading Packages & Estimated Model Outputs for Further Analysis

This section loads the estimation results produced by the S&S 2000 Full Timeline script. The final model outputs were saved at the end of the estimation pipeline and are restored here using the same object names. This ensures full consistency with the original estimation while allowing all subsequent analyses, diagnostics, and summaries to be performed without re-running the estimation step.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}

# Packeges 
library(tibble)
library(FKF)
library(numDeriv)
library(MASS)
library(dplyr)
library(tseries) # jarque.bera.test
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)   # for panel layout
library(gridExtra) # for residual table grob
library(purrr)
library(lubridate)
library(scales)

# Seed
set.seed(42)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE)

# Path to the exported estimation results (relative to this notebook)
RESULTS_DIR <- file.path("results")

FUN_PATH    <- file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "ss_functions_for_analytics_FullTimeline_V2.0.R")
BUNDLE_PATH <- file.path(RESULTS_DIR, "ss_fit_bundle_for_analytics_FullTimeline_V2.0.rds")

stopifnot(file.exists(FUN_PATH))
stopifnot(file.exists(BUNDLE_PATH))

# --- Load function definitions used later (A_fun, make_ss_arrays, etc.)
knit_env <- knitr::knit_global()
sys.source(FUN_PATH, envir = knit_env)

# --- Load saved estimation outputs from Full Timeline
fit_bundle <- readRDS(BUNDLE_PATH)

# --- Restore objects under the names used throughout this Analytics Rmd
theta_hat_SS_FullTimeline_V2.0 <- fit_bundle$theta_hat


Y         <- fit_bundle$Y
Tau       <- fit_bundle$Tau
Delta_t   <- fit_bundle$Delta_t

if (!is.null(fit_bundle$obs_dates)) obs_dates <- fit_bundle$obs_dates
if (!is.null(fit_bundle$kf))        kf_hat    <- fit_bundle$kf
if (!is.null(fit_bundle$best))      best      <- fit_bundle$best

cat("FUN_PATH =", FUN_PATH, "\n")


```

## Step 1: Model Fit Summary and Key Implied Quantities (Schwartz–Smith 2000)

This step provides a concise summary of the estimated two-factor Schwartz–Smith (2000) model using the full available futures price sample. The purpose is to document the overall in-sample fit of the model, report the key structural parameter estimates, and compute economically meaningful implied quantities that are central to the interpretation of the model. This mirrors the role of Table 2 in Schwartz and Smith (2000), which presents parameter estimates and highlights the dynamic properties of the short-term and long-term factors.

The model is estimated on five futures contracts observed over 2,218 weekly observations, resulting in a well-identified specification with twelve estimated parameters. The estimated speed of mean reversion of the short-term deviation factor implies a half-life of approximately 0.83 years, or about 43 weeks. This indicates that transitory price shocks dissipate relatively quickly, though somewhat more slowly than in the original Schwartz and Smith (2000) sample. The volatility of the short-term factor is larger than that of the long-term factor, consistent with the interpretation that short-run fluctuations are more volatile, while the equilibrium component evolves smoothly over time.

The estimated correlation between innovations to the short-term and long-term factors is small but positive, suggesting limited contemporaneous interaction between temporary shocks and long-run movements in prices. The implied long-term risk premium, defined as the difference between the drift parameters of the two factors, is positive and economically meaningful. Measurement error standard deviations decline strongly with maturity, with very small observation noise for longer-dated contracts. This pattern closely aligns with the intuition in Schwartz and Smith (2000) that long-maturity futures prices primarily reflect the persistent equilibrium component rather than short-term fluctuations.

Overall, the parameter estimates and implied quantities are economically sensible and broadly consistent with the findings in Schwartz and Smith (2000), providing a solid foundation for the subsequent statistical diagnostics, pricing checks, and out-of-sample analyses.

```{r step1}
# Parameter object: use S&S 2000 Full Timeline naming and alias to a generic handle
rm(theta_hat)  # prevent accidentally using an old theta_hat from the workspace
theta_hat <- theta_hat_SS_FullTimeline_V2.0

# Observation matrix checks
stopifnot(exists("Y"), is.matrix(Y))
T_len <- ncol(Y)   # number of time periods
n_mat <- nrow(Y)   # number of maturities / contracts

# Structural consistency: one measurement SD per maturity
stopifnot(length(theta_hat$sigma_obs_vec) == n_mat)

message(sprintf("Y matrix: %d maturities × %d observations", n_mat, T_len))
message(sprintf("theta_hat_SS_FullTimeline_V2.0 loaded (kappa=%.3f, sigma_chi=%.3f, sigma_xi=%.3f, rho=%.3f)",
                theta_hat$kappa, theta_hat$sigma_chi, theta_hat$sigma_xi, theta_hat$rho))

# Log-likelihood and information criteria
LL <- if (exists("best") && is.list(best) && !is.null(best$value)) {
  -as.numeric(best$value)  # optim stores NEGATIVE logLik in $value
} else {
  NA_real_
}

# Parameter count: 7 structural + number of measurement SDs
k_par <- 7 + length(theta_hat$sigma_obs_vec)

AIC <- if (is.finite(LL)) (2 * k_par - 2 * LL) else NA_real_

# Derived quantities
half_life_years <- log(2) / theta_hat$kappa
half_life_weeks <- 52 * half_life_years

lambda_xi_implied <- if (!is.null(theta_hat$lambda_xi_implied)) {
  theta_hat$lambda_xi_implied
} else {
  theta_hat$mu - theta_hat$mu_star
}

# Compact output tables
summary_tbl <- tibble(
  metric = c("logLik", "AIC", "n_params", "n_maturities", "n_obs",
             "half_life_years", "half_life_weeks",
             "mu", "mu_star", "lambda_xi_implied", "rho"),
  value  = c(LL, AIC, k_par, n_mat, T_len,
             half_life_years, half_life_weeks,
             theta_hat$mu, theta_hat$mu_star, lambda_xi_implied, theta_hat$rho)
)

params_tbl <- tibble(
  parameter = c("kappa", "sigma_chi", "sigma_xi", "rho",
                "mu", "mu_star", "lambda_chi", "lambda_xi_implied"),
  estimate  = c(theta_hat$kappa, theta_hat$sigma_chi, theta_hat$sigma_xi, theta_hat$rho,
                theta_hat$mu, theta_hat$mu_star, theta_hat$lambda_chi, lambda_xi_implied)
)

maturity_months <- c(1, 5, 9, 13, 17)

stopifnot(length(theta_hat$sigma_obs_vec) == length(maturity_months))

sigma_obs_tbl <- tibble(
  maturity_months = maturity_months,
  sigma_obs       = as.numeric(theta_hat$sigma_obs_vec)
)


print(summary_tbl)
print(params_tbl)
print(sigma_obs_tbl)

```

## Step 2: Standard Errors and Statistical Uncertainty of Model Parameters

This step assesses the statistical precision of the estimated parameters of the Schwartz–Smith (2000) two-factor model. While Step 1 documented point estimates and implied quantities, Step 2 focuses on quantifying estimation uncertainty using standard errors and confidence intervals. This analysis corresponds conceptually to the statistical interpretation of parameter estimates in Schwartz and Smith (2000), although the original paper does not explicitly report full covariance matrices.

Standard errors are obtained from the inverse Hessian of the log-likelihood function evaluated at the maximum likelihood estimates. Because the model is estimated in a transformed (packed) parameter space to enforce parameter constraints, the covariance matrix is mapped back to economically meaningful parameters using the delta method. This ensures that uncertainty measures are fully consistent with the estimation methodology and the nonlinear parameter transformations used in the model.

The results indicate that the core structural parameters of the model are estimated with high precision. In particular, the speed of mean reversion of the short-term deviation factor is tightly identified, leading to a precisely estimated half-life of approximately 43 weeks with a narrow confidence interval. The volatility parameters of both the short-term and long-term factors are also estimated precisely, reflecting the strong information content of the futures term structure over the long sample period. In contrast, the market price of risk parameters exhibit substantially higher uncertainty. The confidence intervals for both the short-term and long-term risk premia include zero, consistent with the identification challenges emphasized in Schwartz and Smith (2000).

Measurement error standard deviations are estimated very precisely for short- and medium-dated contracts, and remain small for longer maturities. The strong decline in measurement error with maturity is statistically robust and reinforces the interpretation that longer-dated futures prices primarily reflect the persistent equilibrium component rather than short-term fluctuations. Overall, the precision results confirm that the main dynamic features of the Schwartz–Smith model are well identified in the data, while risk-premium parameters are more weakly determined, in line with the original paper’s discussion.

```{r step2}
# --- 1) Numerical Hessian of NEGATIVE log-likelihood at optimum ------------ #
# In S&S 2000 Full Timeline: loglik(p, Y, Tau, Delta_t) returns NEGATIVE log-likelihood.
H <- numDeriv::hessian(
  func = function(p) loglik(p, Y = Y, Tau = Tau, Delta_t = Delta_t),
  x    = best$par
)

# Symmetrize to reduce numerical jitter
H <- 0.5 * (H + t(H))

# --- 2) Invert Hessian -> covariance of packed parameters ------------------ #
vcov_packed <- tryCatch(solve(H), error = function(e) NULL)
if (is.null(vcov_packed)) {
  message("Hessian near-singular; using MASS::ginv pseudoinverse.")
  vcov_packed <- MASS::ginv(H)
}

# --- 3) Map packed parameters -> natural parameters (via unpack) ----------- #
# This uses the unpack() function from S&S 2000 Full Timeline to ensure consistency.
nat_from_p <- function(p) {
  th <- unpack(p)
  c(
    kappa      = th$kappa,
    sigma_chi  = th$sigma_chi,
    sigma_xi   = th$sigma_xi,
    rho        = th$rho,
    mu         = th$mu,
    mu_star    = th$mu_star,
    lambda_chi = th$lambda_chi,
    lambda_xi  = th$mu - th$mu_star,          # implied in SS2000
    sigma_obs_1  = th$sigma_obs_vec[1],
    sigma_obs_2  = th$sigma_obs_vec[2],
    sigma_obs_3  = th$sigma_obs_vec[3],
    sigma_obs_4  = th$sigma_obs_vec[4],
    sigma_obs_5  = th$sigma_obs_vec[5]
  )
}

p_hat   <- best$par
nat_hat <- nat_from_p(p_hat)

# --- 4) Jacobian: d(natural) / d(packed) ---------------------------------- #
G <- numDeriv::jacobian(func = nat_from_p, x = p_hat)

# --- 5) Delta-method covariance in natural space -------------------------- #
vcov_nat <- G %*% vcov_packed %*% t(G)

rn <- names(nat_hat)
dimnames(vcov_nat) <- list(rn, rn)

se_nat <- sqrt(pmax(diag(vcov_nat), 0))  # guard against tiny negative diag
z <- qnorm(0.975)

parameter_se <- tibble(
  parameter = rn,
  estimate  = as.numeric(nat_hat),
  se        = as.numeric(se_nat),
  ci95_lo   = as.numeric(nat_hat - z * se_nat),
  ci95_hi   = as.numeric(nat_hat + z * se_nat)
)

# --- 6) Derived quantity: half-life of mean reversion ---------------------- #
# half_life_years = ln(2)/kappa
var_kappa <- vcov_nat["kappa", "kappa"]

half_life_years <- log(2) / nat_hat["kappa"]
dh_dkappa <- -log(2) / (nat_hat["kappa"]^2)

half_life_se_years <- abs(dh_dkappa) * sqrt(max(var_kappa, 0))

derived_se <- tibble(
  derived  = c("half_life_years", "half_life_weeks", "mu", "mu_star", "lambda_xi"),
  estimate = c(as.numeric(half_life_years),
               as.numeric(half_life_years * 52),
               nat_hat["mu"], nat_hat["mu_star"], nat_hat["lambda_xi"]),
  se       = c(as.numeric(half_life_se_years),
               as.numeric(half_life_se_years * 52),
               se_nat[match("mu", rn)],
               se_nat[match("mu_star", rn)],
               se_nat[match("lambda_xi", rn)]),
  ci95_lo  = c(as.numeric(half_life_years - z * half_life_se_years),
               as.numeric((half_life_years - z * half_life_se_years) * 52),
               nat_hat["mu"] - z * se_nat[match("mu", rn)],
               nat_hat["mu_star"] - z * se_nat[match("mu_star", rn)],
               nat_hat["lambda_xi"] - z * se_nat[match("lambda_xi", rn)]),
  ci95_hi  = c(as.numeric(half_life_years + z * half_life_se_years),
               as.numeric((half_life_years + z * half_life_se_years) * 52),
               nat_hat["mu"] + z * se_nat[match("mu", rn)],
               nat_hat["mu_star"] + z * se_nat[match("mu_star", rn)],
               nat_hat["lambda_xi"] + z * se_nat[match("lambda_xi", rn)])
)

# --- 7) Add SEs to Step 1 tables (if they exist) --------------------------- #
if (exists("params_tbl") && is.data.frame(params_tbl)) {
  params_tbl <- params_tbl %>%
    left_join(
      parameter_se %>%
        filter(parameter %in% c("kappa","sigma_chi","sigma_xi","rho","mu","mu_star","lambda_chi","lambda_xi")) %>%
        dplyr::select(parameter, std_error = se, ci95_lo, ci95_hi),
      by = "parameter"
    )
}


# Step 1 sigma_obs_tbl uses maturity_months; map it to sigma_obs_1..5
if (exists("sigma_obs_tbl") && is.data.frame(sigma_obs_tbl)) {
  sigma_obs_tbl <- sigma_obs_tbl %>%
    mutate(maturity_id = row_number()) %>%
    left_join(
      parameter_se %>%
        filter(grepl("^sigma_obs_", parameter)) %>%
        mutate(maturity_id = as.integer(sub("sigma_obs_", "", parameter))) %>%
        dplyr::select(maturity_id, std_error = se, ci95_lo, ci95_hi),
      by = "maturity_id"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(-maturity_id)
}

# --- 8) Display ------------------------------------------------------------ #
parameter_se
derived_se
if (exists("params_tbl")) params_tbl
if (exists("sigma_obs_tbl")) sigma_obs_tbl

invisible(list(
  vcov_packed  = vcov_packed,
  vcov_nat     = vcov_nat,
  parameter_se = parameter_se,
  derived_se   = derived_se,
  params_tbl   = if (exists("params_tbl")) params_tbl else NULL,
  sigma_obs_tbl = if (exists("sigma_obs_tbl")) sigma_obs_tbl else NULL
))

```

## Step 3: Innovation and Fit Error Diagnostics Across Contract Maturities

This step evaluates the in-sample fit of the estimated Schwartz–Smith (2000) model by analyzing forecast errors and fit residuals across futures maturities. While previous steps focused on parameter estimation and statistical precision, Step 3 assesses how well the model reproduces observed futures prices at different points along the term structure. This mirrors the spirit of Table 3 in Schwartz and Smith (2000), which summarizes pricing errors by maturity for futures contracts.

The first part of the analysis examines one-step-ahead forecast errors (Kalman filter innovations). For each maturity, root mean squared errors (RMSE) and mean absolute errors (MAE) are computed and compared to the model-implied innovation standard deviations and the estimated measurement error variances. The results show that forecast errors decline systematically with maturity, indicating that short-dated contracts are more volatile and harder to predict, while longer-dated futures are more stable and largely driven by the persistent equilibrium component. Innovation RMSEs are closely aligned with the model-implied innovation standard deviations, suggesting that the state-space specification captures the overall scale of forecast uncertainty well.

The second part of the step evaluates fit errors using filtered state estimates, corresponding to the model’s real-time fitted values. Residuals are computed as the difference between observed log futures prices and model-implied prices based on the filtered states. Across maturities, mean errors are close to zero, indicating negligible systematic bias. The dispersion and mean absolute errors are small and closely track the estimated measurement error standard deviations, consistent with the interpretation that remaining pricing errors primarily reflect measurement noise rather than model misspecification.

Finally, the same fit diagnostics are repeated using smoothed state estimates, which condition on the full sample and therefore provide the best in-sample reconstruction of latent factors. As expected, smoothed-fit residuals are slightly smaller than filtered-fit residuals, while exhibiting very similar patterns across maturities. The close agreement between filtered and smoothed results confirms that the model is stable over time and that most pricing information is already incorporated contemporaneously.

Overall, the in-sample diagnostics confirm that the Schwartz–Smith model provides an accurate and unbiased representation of futures prices across the term structure. Pricing errors decrease with maturity, residuals are centered around zero, and their magnitude is consistent with the estimated measurement error variances. These findings closely align with the empirical behavior reported in Schwartz and Smith (2000) and provide a solid foundation for the subsequent structural and out-of-sample analyses.

```{r step3}
#############################################################################
# STEP 3a — RMSE by maturity (innovations)
#############################################################################

# Basic checks
stopifnot(exists("kf_hat"), exists("Y"))
stopifnot(is.list(kf_hat), is.matrix(Y))

n_mat <- nrow(Y)   # number of maturities (rows of Y)
T_len <- ncol(Y)   # number of time points

vt <- kf_hat$vt    # one-step-ahead forecast errors (innovations)
Ft <- kf_hat$Ft    # innovation covariance matrices

# If these are missing, this whole step is meaningless
stopifnot(!is.null(vt), !is.null(Ft))

# RMSE/MAE of innovations per maturity (how large are forecast errors by row)
RMSE_maturity <- sqrt(rowMeans(vt^2, na.rm = TRUE))
MAE_maturity  <- rowMeans(abs(vt),  na.rm = TRUE)

# Model-implied SD of innovations: sqrt(diag(F_t)), averaged over time
innov_sd_t <- sapply(seq_len(T_len), function(tt) sqrt(diag(Ft[, , tt])))
avg_innov_SD <- rowMeans(innov_sd_t, na.rm = TRUE)

# Labels for readability (assumes the 5-contract setup)
maturity_months <- c(1, 5, 9, 13, 17)
stopifnot(length(maturity_months) == n_mat)  # prevents mislabeling

rmse_tbl <- tibble(
  maturity_months = maturity_months,
  RMSE            = RMSE_maturity,
  MAE             = MAE_maturity,
  avg_innov_SD    = avg_innov_SD,
  sigma_obs       = as.numeric(theta_hat$sigma_obs_vec)  # measurement noise per maturity
)

rmse_tbl
invisible(rmse_tbl)


#############################################################################
# STEP 3b(i) — Fit errors using FILTERED states (x_{t|t})
#############################################################################

# Basic checks
# - Tau and Delta_t are needed to rebuild Zt and ct if ss_hat is not in memory
stopifnot(exists("Tau"), exists("Delta_t"))
stopifnot(is.matrix(Tau), is.numeric(Delta_t), length(Delta_t) == 1)

# Build state-space arrays (Z_t and c_t) if not already available
# This keeps the analytics self-contained after loading the S&S 2000 Full Timeline RDS.
if (!exists("ss_hat")) {
  stopifnot(exists("make_ss_arrays"))
  ss_hat <- make_ss_arrays(theta_hat, Tau, Delta_t)
}

# Filtered state estimates from the Kalman filter: x_{t|t}
# (2 states: chi_t and xi_t)
x_filt <- kf_hat$att
stopifnot(!is.null(x_filt))  # without states we can't fit anything

# Fitted observation using filtered states:
# y_hat_{t|t} = c_t + Z_t * x_{t|t}
y_hat_fit <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_mat, ncol = T_len)
for (t in seq_len(T_len)) {
  y_hat_fit[, t] <- ss_hat$ct[, t] + ss_hat$Zt[, , t] %*% x_filt[, t]
}

# Fit residuals in log-price space (same units as Y)
fit_resid <- Y - y_hat_fit

# Summary diagnostics by maturity
fit_mean <- rowMeans(fit_resid, na.rm = TRUE)           # average bias
fit_sd   <- apply(fit_resid, 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE)       # dispersion
fit_mae  <- rowMeans(abs(fit_resid), na.rm = TRUE)      # typical absolute error

table3_like_filtered <- tibble(
  maturity_months = maturity_months,
  mean            = fit_mean,
  sd              = fit_sd,
  MAE             = fit_mae,
  sigma_obs       = as.numeric(theta_hat$sigma_obs_vec)
)

table3_like_filtered
invisible(table3_like_filtered)


#############################################################################
# STEP 3b(ii) — Fit errors using SMOOTHED states (x_{t|T})
#############################################################################

# Basic checks
stopifnot(!is.null(kf_hat$Ptt), !is.null(kf_hat$Pt), !is.null(kf_hat$at))

# Start smoother at filtered estimates (these will be overwritten going backwards)
xs <- kf_hat$att
Ps <- kf_hat$Ptt

# Transition matrix for the latent state dynamics (2x2)
G <- ss_hat$Tt[, , 1]

# Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother: backward recursion t = T-1,...,1
for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {

  Ptt_t <- kf_hat$Ptt[, , t]       # P_{t|t}
  Pt1_t <- kf_hat$Pt [ , , t + 1]  # P_{t+1|t}
  a_pred_next <- kf_hat$at[, t + 1]# a_{t+1|t}

  # Smoother gain: J_t = P_{t|t} G' (P_{t+1|t})^{-1}
  Jt <- tryCatch(
    Ptt_t %*% t(G) %*% solve(Pt1_t),
    error = function(e) Ptt_t %*% t(G) %*% MASS::ginv(Pt1_t)
  )

  # Smoothed mean update: a_{t|T}
  xs[, t] <- kf_hat$att[, t] + Jt %*% (xs[, t + 1] - a_pred_next)

  # Smoothed covariance update: P_{t|T}
  Ps[, , t] <- Ptt_t + Jt %*% (Ps[, , t + 1] - Pt1_t) %*% t(Jt)
}

# Fitted observation using smoothed states:
# y_hat_{t|T} = c_t + Z_t * x_{t|T}
y_hat_sm <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_mat, ncol = T_len)
for (t in seq_len(T_len)) {
  y_hat_sm[, t] <- ss_hat$ct[, t] + ss_hat$Zt[, , t] %*% xs[, t]
}

# Residuals using smoothed fit (typically smaller than filtered-fit residuals)
resid_sm <- Y - y_hat_sm

fit_mean_sm <- rowMeans(resid_sm, na.rm = TRUE)
fit_sd_sm   <- apply(resid_sm, 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
fit_mae_sm  <- rowMeans(abs(resid_sm), na.rm = TRUE)

table3_like_smoothed <- tibble(
  maturity_months = maturity_months,
  mean            = fit_mean_sm,
  sd              = fit_sd_sm,
  MAE             = fit_mae_sm,
  sigma_obs       = as.numeric(theta_hat$sigma_obs_vec)
)

table3_like_smoothed
invisible(table3_like_smoothed)

```

## Step 4: Diagnostics of Standardized Innovations

This step evaluates whether the one-step-ahead forecast errors produced by the Kalman filter behave in line with the assumptions of the Schwartz–Smith (2000) state-space model. Innovations are standardized using their model-implied conditional variances and should, under correct specification, have mean zero, unit variance, and limited serial and cross-sectional dependence.

The standardized innovations exhibit means close to zero and standard deviations near one across all maturities, indicating that the model captures the scale of forecast uncertainty well and shows little systematic bias. Normality is strongly rejected for all contracts, which is typical for commodity futures data and consistent with the empirical findings in Schwartz and Smith (2000).

Ljung–Box tests reveal remaining serial correlation, particularly for short maturities and at longer lags, suggesting that some short-run dynamics are not fully absorbed by the two-factor structure. In addition, standardized innovations remain strongly correlated across maturities, reflecting substantial common shocks in futures prices that are only partially captured by the latent factors.

Overall, these diagnostics suggest that the model provides a reasonable but stylized representation of the data: it captures the main dynamics and volatility structure of the futures curve while leaving some residual dependence, in line with the scope and intent of the Schwartz–Smith framework.

```{r step4}
#############################################################################
# STEP 4 — Residual diagnostics on standardized innovations
#############################################################################

# --- Inputs created upstream (S&S 2000 Full Timeline -> analytics) ----------
vt <- kf_hat$vt   # innovations: v_{t} = y_t - E[y_t | t-1}  (maturities x time)
Ft <- kf_hat$Ft   # innovation covariance matrices F_t       (m x m x time)

# Required inputs: if these are missing, the diagnostics are not defined
stopifnot(!is.null(vt), !is.null(Ft))

n_mat <- nrow(Y)      # number of maturities (rows)
T_len <- ncol(Y)      # number of time points (columns)

# Ljung–Box at lag 20 needs a reasonable sample length
stopifnot(T_len >= 25)

# Labels only (for readable tables); keep consistent with the rest of the thesis
maturity_months <- c(1, 5, 9, 13, 17)
stopifnot(length(maturity_months) == n_mat)

# --- 1) Standardized innovations z_{m,t} -----------------------------------
# For each maturity m and time t:
#   z_{m,t} = v_{m,t} / sqrt(F_{m,m,t})
# If the model is well specified, z should look roughly like iid N(0,1).

# Extract diag(F_t) for each t as an (m x T) matrix
Ft_diag <- sapply(seq_len(dim(Ft)[3]), function(tt) diag(Ft[, , tt]))

# Convert variances to standard deviations; pmax() avoids division by ~0
innov_sd_t <- sqrt(pmax(Ft_diag, 1e-12))

# Standardize the innovations maturity-by-maturity
z <- vt / innov_sd_t

# --- 2) Distribution diagnostics per maturity ------------------------------
# mean_z ~ 0: no systematic forecast bias
# sd_z   ~ 1: model-implied forecast-error variance matches realized variance
# t_pval: test mean(z) = 0
# jb_pval: Jarque–Bera normality test (often rejected in commodities; still informative)

dist_tbl <- tibble(
  maturity_months = maturity_months,
  mean_z = rowMeans(z, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd_z   = apply(z, 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE),
  t_pval = sapply(seq_len(nrow(z)), function(i) t.test(z[i, ])$p.value),
  jb_pval = sapply(seq_len(nrow(z)), function(i)
    tryCatch(tseries::jarque.bera.test(z[i, ])$p.value, error = function(e) NA_real_))
)

# --- 3) Serial correlation diagnostics (Ljung–Box on z) ---------------------
# Standardized innovations should be approximately uncorrelated over time
# if the state dynamics are correctly captured.

lb_tbl <- tibble(
  maturity_months = maturity_months,
  lb_pval_lag5  = sapply(seq_len(nrow(z)), function(i) Box.test(z[i, ], lag = 5,  type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value),
  lb_pval_lag10 = sapply(seq_len(nrow(z)), function(i) Box.test(z[i, ], lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value),
  lb_pval_lag20 = sapply(seq_len(nrow(z)), function(i) Box.test(z[i, ], lag = 20, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
)

# --- 4) Cross-maturity correlation diagnostics -----------------------------
# After accounting for the two factors, residual shocks should ideally be weakly
# correlated across maturities. Large off-diagonals suggest remaining common shocks
# not captured by the model/measurement structure.

cor_z <- cor(t(z), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")   # maturity x maturity correlation
offdiag <- cor_z[upper.tri(cor_z)]

cross_summary <- tibble(
  stat  = c("mean_abs_offdiag", "max_abs_offdiag"),
  value = c(mean(abs(offdiag), na.rm = TRUE), max(abs(offdiag), na.rm = TRUE))
)

# --- 5) Display outputs -----------------------------------------------------

dist_tbl
lb_tbl
cor_z
cross_summary

invisible(list(
  standardized_innovations_summary = dist_tbl,
  ljung_box_pvalues                = lb_tbl,
  cross_maturity_correlation       = cor_z,
  cross_maturity_summary           = cross_summary,
  z                                = z   # return standardized innovations for later plots/tests
))

```

## Step 5:Model-Implied Spot and Equilibrium Price Dynamics

This step illustrates the core economic decomposition of the Schwartz–Smith (2000) model by separating the spot price into a transitory short-term component and a persistent long-term equilibrium component. Using smoothed state estimates from the Kalman smoother, the equilibrium price is constructed from the long-term factor alone, while the model-implied spot price combines both latent factors. This corresponds directly to Figure 4 in Schwartz and Smith (2000).

The resulting figure shows that short-term price fluctuations are large but short-lived, while the equilibrium price evolves smoothly over time, capturing gradual shifts in long-run fundamentals. Periods of sharp price spikes are therefore primarily driven by the short-term factor, whereas longer-run movements reflect changes in the equilibrium level. Overall, the decomposition closely mirrors the dynamics documented in the original paper and confirms the economic interpretation of the two-factor structure.

```{r step5}
#############################################################################
# STEP 5 — Spot vs Equilibrium (Figure 4 style)
#############################################################################

# --- 0) Inputs and time index ------------------------------------------------

stopifnot(exists("kf_hat"), is.list(kf_hat), !is.null(kf_hat$att))
stopifnot(is.matrix(kf_hat$att), nrow(kf_hat$att) == 2)

T_len <- ncol(kf_hat$att)

# Use obs_dates from S&S 2000 Full Timeline if available; otherwise fall back to 1..T
dates <- if (exists("obs_dates")) {
  d <- as.Date(obs_dates)
  if (length(d) != T_len) d <- tail(d, T_len)  # align if needed
  d
} else {
  seq_len(T_len)
}

# --- 1) RTS smoothing (compute xs only if missing) --------------------------

# We want smoothed states x_{t|T}. If xs already exists, we reuse it.
if (!exists("xs")) {

  # FKF objects needed for RTS recursion
  stopifnot(!is.null(kf_hat$Ptt), !is.null(kf_hat$Pt), !is.null(kf_hat$at))
  stopifnot(exists("ss_hat"), is.list(ss_hat), !is.null(ss_hat$Tt))

  xs <- kf_hat$att              # start from filtered state means x_{t|t}
  Ps <- kf_hat$Ptt              # and filtered covariances P_{t|t}
  G  <- ss_hat$Tt[, , 1]        # state transition matrix (2x2), time-invariant here

  # Backward recursion: t = T-1, ..., 1
  for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {

    Ptt_t <- kf_hat$Ptt[, , t]        # P_{t|t}
    Pt1_t <- kf_hat$Pt [ , , t + 1]   # P_{t+1|t}
    a_pred_next <- kf_hat$at[, t + 1] # a_{t+1|t}

    # Smoother gain J_t = P_{t|t} G' (P_{t+1|t})^{-1}
    Jt <- tryCatch(
      Ptt_t %*% t(G) %*% solve(Pt1_t),
      error = function(e) Ptt_t %*% t(G) %*% MASS::ginv(Pt1_t)
    )

    # Smoothed mean: a_{t|T} = a_{t|t} + J_t (a_{t+1|T} - a_{t+1|t})
    xs[, t] <- kf_hat$att[, t] + Jt %*% (xs[, t + 1] - a_pred_next)

    # Smoothed covariance: P_{t|T} = P_{t|t} + J_t (P_{t+1|T} - P_{t+1|t}) J_t'
    Ps[, , t] <- Ptt_t + Jt %*% (Ps[, , t + 1] - Pt1_t) %*% t(Jt)
  }
}

# --- 2) Construct equilibrium and spot in levels ----------------------------

chi_sm <- as.numeric(xs[1, ])            # chi_t (short-term deviation)
xi_sm  <- as.numeric(xs[2, ])            # xi_t  (equilibrium level)

df_fig <- tibble(
  time     = dates,
  eq_price = exp(xi_sm),                 # equilibrium component = exp(xi_t)
  spot_est = exp(xi_sm + chi_sm)         # spot estimate        = exp(xi_t + chi_t)
)

# --- 3) Reshape and plot -----------------------------------------------------
# Build plotting data (long format) for ggplot
plot_df <- df_fig %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(spot_est, eq_price),
    names_to = "series",
    values_to = "price"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    series = factor(
      series,
      levels = c("spot_est", "eq_price"),
      labels = c("Spot (model)", "Equilibrium (model)")
    )
  )

p_fig <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = time, y = price)) +
  geom_line(
    data = subset(plot_df, series == "Spot (model)"),
    aes(colour = "Spot (model)", linetype = "Spot (model)"),
    linewidth = 0.9   # ↑ larger dots
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = subset(plot_df, series == "Equilibrium (model)"),
    aes(colour = "Equilibrium (model)", linetype = "Equilibrium (model)"),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Spot (model)" = "black",
      "Equilibrium (model)" = "black"
    )
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "Spot (model)" = "dotted",
      "Equilibrium (model)" = "solid"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Model-implied Spot vs Equilibrium Price",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Price (levels)",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9)
  )

p_fig

```

## Step 6: Pricing Identity and Futures Curve Overlay

This step evaluates the internal pricing consistency of the estimated Schwartz–Smith (2000) model by directly comparing observed futures prices to model-implied prices across maturities and time. Rather than focusing on time-series fit alone, this analysis assesses whether the estimated latent factors and parameters can accurately reconstruct the cross-sectional shape of the futures curve, which is a central implication of the model’s no-arbitrage pricing structure.

Using the smoothed state estimates of the short-term deviation and long-term equilibrium components, the model-implied futures curve is reconstructed analytically for selected weeks. Smoothed states condition on the full sample of observations and therefore provide the statistically most precise reconstruction of the underlying latent price components implied by the model. Their use is appropriate in this context, as the objective is not real-time forecasting but the economic interpretation and internal consistency of the estimated pricing structure.

For each date, observed futures prices at traded maturities are overlaid with (i) the model-implied prices at those maturities and (ii) a smooth model-implied curve evaluated over a dense maturity grid. This corresponds closely to the pricing identity discussed in Schwartz and Smith (2000) and provides a stringent economic validation of the estimated model. In addition to the smoothed-state analysis, the same overlays are constructed using filtered state estimates, which condition only on information available up to each date but rely on the same full-sample parameter estimates. Comparing filtered and smoothed reconstructions allows for an assessment of how strongly future observations revise the inferred latent states, holding the model parameters fixed. The resulting curves are visually very similar, indicating that the cross-section of futures prices already pins down the latent factors tightly in real time, with limited additional revision from future data.

The broad-sweep panels show that the model captures the overall level, slope, and curvature of the futures curve well across different market regimes, including periods of contango and backwardation. Even over the extended sample period, the fitted curves closely track observed prices, indicating that the estimated factor dynamics translate consistently into cross-sectional pricing implications.

The focused-episode panels highlight the model’s performance during periods of heightened market stress and structural change, such as the early 2000s, the Global Financial Crisis, the COVID-19 shock, and recent energy market disruptions. While small deviations at short maturities occasionally arise, the model continues to reproduce the dominant shape of the futures curve, suggesting that most pricing variation is captured by the two latent factors.

Overall, these results confirm that the estimated Schwartz–Smith model is internally coherent from a pricing perspective. The same parameters and latent factor structure that explain time-series dynamics also generate economically sensible futures curves across a wide range of maturities and market conditions, closely mirroring the behavior documented in the original paper.

```{r step6}
#############################################################################
# STEP 6 — SmoothedStates 
#############################################################################

# --- 0) Small utilities -----------------------------------------------------#
# Ensure smoothed states xs (2×T) and aligned date vector
.ensure_smoothed <- function() {
  stopifnot(exists("kf_hat"), exists("ss_hat"), is.matrix(kf_hat$att))
  T_len <- ncol(kf_hat$att)
  # Dates: prefer obs_dates; fallback = colnames(Y); else integer index
  dates <- NULL
  if (exists("obs_dates")) {
    dates <- as.Date(obs_dates); dates <- tail(dates, T_len)
  } else if (exists("Y") && !is.null(colnames(Y))) {
    try_dates <- try(as.Date(colnames(Y)), silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(try_dates, "try-error") && !any(is.na(try_dates)))
      dates <- tail(try_dates, T_len)
  }
  if (is.null(dates)) dates <- seq_len(T_len)
  
  if (!exists("xs")) {
    xs <<- kf_hat$att
    Ps <- kf_hat$Ptt
    G  <- ss_hat$Tt[, , 1]
    for (t in (T_len - 1):1) {
      Ptt_t <- kf_hat$Ptt[, , t]
      Pt1_t <- kf_hat$Pt [ , , t + 1]
      Jt <- tryCatch(Ptt_t %*% t(G) %*% solve(Pt1_t),
                     error = function(e) Ptt_t %*% t(G) %*% MASS::ginv(Pt1_t))
      a_pred_next <- kf_hat$at[, t + 1]
      xs[, t]   <<- kf_hat$att[, t] + Jt %*% (xs[, t + 1] - a_pred_next)
      Ps[, , t] <- Ptt_t + Jt %*% (Ps[, , t + 1] - Pt1_t) %*% t(Jt)
    }
  }
  list(dates = dates, T_len = T_len)
}

# One overlay (observed vs model) for time index t_idx
.overlay_plot_idx <- function(t_idx, in_levels = FALSE) {
  h <- .ensure_smoothed(); dates <- h$dates; T_len <- h$T_len
  stopifnot(t_idx >= 1, t_idx <= T_len)
  m  <- if (exists("Y") && is.matrix(Y)) nrow(Y) else dim(ss_hat$Zt)[1]
  
  chi_t <- xs[1, t_idx]; xi_t <- xs[2, t_idx]
  Z_t <- ss_hat$Zt[, , t_idx]; c_t <- ss_hat$ct[, t_idx]
  y_hat_log <- as.numeric(c_t + Z_t %*% c(chi_t, xi_t))
  y_obs_log <- as.numeric(Y[, t_idx])
  
  # τ for x-axis
  tau_pts <- if (exists("Tau") && is.matrix(Tau) && ncol(Tau) >= t_idx) Tau[, t_idx]
  else if (exists("ranks")) ranks/12 else seq_len(m)/12
  
  # Smooth model curve via A_fun (from base)
  tau_grid <- seq(0, max(tau_pts, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 200)
  A_grid <- A_fun(
    T         = tau_grid,
    kappa     = theta_hat$kappa,
    mu_star   = theta_hat$mu_star,
    sigma_chi = theta_hat$sigma_chi,
    sigma_xi  = theta_hat$sigma_xi,
    rho       = theta_hat$rho,
    lambda_chi= theta_hat$lambda_chi
  )
  y_grid_log <- A_grid + exp(-theta_hat$kappa * tau_grid) * chi_t + xi_t
  
  if (isTRUE(in_levels)) {
    y_obs <- exp(y_obs_log); y_hat <- exp(y_hat_log); y_line <- exp(y_grid_log); ylab <- "Price (levels)"
  } else {
    y_obs <- y_obs_log;      y_hat <- y_hat_log;      y_line <- y_grid_log;      ylab <- "log price"
  }
  
  df_pts  <- tibble(maturity_m = 12 * tau_pts, observed = y_obs, model = y_hat)
  df_line <- tibble(maturity_m = 12 * tau_grid, model = y_line)
  
  ggplot() +
    geom_line(data = df_line, aes(maturity_m, model), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = df_pts,  aes(maturity_m, observed),
               shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black", size = 2.6, stroke = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = df_pts,  aes(maturity_m, model),
               shape = 19, colour = "black", size = 1.8) +
    labs(title = format(dates[t_idx], "%d %b %Y"),
         x = "Maturity (months)", y = ylab) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 10)
}

# Pick N indices evenly spaced inside [from, to]
.pick_spaced <- function(from, to, n = 6) {
  h <- .ensure_smoothed(); dates <- h$dates
  from <- as.Date(from); to <- as.Date(to)
  idx <- which(dates >= from & dates <= to)
  if (!length(idx)) return(integer(0))
  if (length(idx) <= n) return(idx)
  unique(round(seq(min(idx), max(idx), length.out = n)))
}

# Pick nearest to fixed mm-dd in each year within [from, to] (capped to n_max)
.pick_mmdd <- function(from, to, mm = 6, dd = 15, n_max = 6) {
  h <- .ensure_smoothed(); dates <- h$dates
  from <- as.Date(from); to <- as.Date(to)
  yrs <- intersect(unique(year(dates)), year(from):year(to))
  idx <- integer(0)
  for (yy in yrs) {
    target <- as.Date(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d", yy, mm, dd))
    cand   <- which(year(dates) == yy)
    if (length(cand)) idx <- c(idx, cand[ which.min(abs(dates[cand] - target)) ])
  }
  if (length(idx) > n_max) idx <- unique(round(seq(min(idx), max(idx), length.out = n_max)))
  idx
}

# Draw a grid of overlays; print to screen; optionally save if savepath is given
.print_grid <- function(idx, title = NULL, ncol = 3, in_levels = FALSE, savepath = NULL) {
  plots <- lapply(idx, function(i) .overlay_plot_idx(i, in_levels = in_levels))
  if (length(plots) == 0) stop("No plots to show for the chosen window.")
  grid <- cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = plots, ncol = ncol)
  fig  <- if (!is.null(title)) {
    top <- cowplot::ggdraw() + cowplot::draw_label(title, fontface = "bold", x = 0, hjust = 0)
    cowplot::plot_grid(top, grid, ncol = 1, rel_heights = c(0.08, 0.92))
  } else grid
  print(fig)
  if (!is.null(savepath)) {
    dir.create(dirname(savepath), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    ggsave(savepath, fig, width = 14, height = max(6, ceiling(length(plots)/ncol)*2.2), dpi = 300)
  }
  invisible(fig)
}

# Set A: broad sweep (one representative week per subperiod)
plot_set_A <- function(in_levels = FALSE, savepath = NULL) {
  windows <- list(
    c("1990-01-01","1994-12-31"),
    c("1995-01-01","1999-12-31"),
    c("2000-01-01","2004-12-31"),
    c("2005-01-01","2009-12-31"),
    c("2010-01-01","2014-12-31"),
    c("2015-01-01","2019-12-31")
  )
  idx <- unlist(lapply(windows, function(w) .pick_spaced(w[1], w[2], n = 1)))
  .print_grid(idx, title = "Observed vs Model — Broad Sweep (1990→2019)",
              ncol = 3, in_levels = in_levels, savepath = savepath)
}

# Set B: focused/modern episodes (one representative per window, near mid-year)
plot_set_B <- function(in_levels = FALSE, savepath = NULL) {
  windows <- list(
    c("2000-01-01","2002-12-31"),
    c("2008-01-01","2009-12-31"),
    c("2014-06-01","2016-12-31"),
    c("2020-01-01","2021-12-31"),
    c("2022-01-01","2023-12-31"),
    c("2024-01-01", as.character(max(.ensure_smoothed()$dates)))
  )
  idx <- unlist(lapply(windows, function(w) .pick_mmdd(w[1], w[2], mm = 6, dd = 15, n_max = 1)))
  .print_grid(idx, title = "Observed vs Model — Focused Episodes",
              ncol = 3, in_levels = in_levels, savepath = savepath)
}

# --- 2) Custom 6-panel helpers ---------------------------------------------#

# One window → 6 panels (evenly spaced or one per year near mm-dd)
plot_window6 <- function(from, to, picker = c("spaced","mmdd"),
                         in_levels = FALSE, savepath = NULL) {
  picker <- match.arg(picker)
  idx <- if (picker == "spaced") .pick_spaced(from, to, n = 6)
  else .pick_mmdd(from, to, n_max = 6)
  .print_grid(idx, title = sprintf("Observed vs Model — %s to %s", from, to),
              ncol = 3, in_levels = in_levels, savepath = savepath)
}

# Six explicit dates or numeric indices → 6 panels
plot_dates6 <- function(dates_or_indices, in_levels = FALSE, savepath = NULL) {
  h <- .ensure_smoothed(); dates <- h$dates
  idx <- sapply(dates_or_indices, function(x) {
    if (is.numeric(x)) as.integer(x) else which.min(abs(dates - as.Date(x)))
  })
  .print_grid(idx, title = "Observed vs Model — Selected Weeks",
              ncol = 3, in_levels = in_levels, savepath = savepath)
}

# --- 3) A couple of extra long-sample visuals (optional) -------------------#

# States over time (χ_t and ξ_t; log levels by default)
plot_states_long <- function(in_levels = FALSE) {
  h <- .ensure_smoothed(); dates <- h$dates
  chi <- as.numeric(xs[1, ]); xi <- as.numeric(xs[2, ])
  df <- tibble(date = dates,
               chi  = if (in_levels) exp(chi) else chi,
               xi   = if (in_levels) exp(xi)  else xi) |>
    pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "state", values_to = "value")
  ggplot(df, aes(date, value, color = state)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, show.legend = TRUE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("black","grey40"), labels = c("Short-term χₜ","Equilibrium ξₜ")) +
    labs(title = "State Dynamics", x = NULL, y = if (in_levels) "Level" else "Log level", color = NULL) +
    theme_classic()
}

# Rolling 1-step RMSE by maturity (default 52-week window) using innovations
plot_rolling_rmse <- function(window_weeks = 52) {
  stopifnot(is.matrix(kf_hat$vt))
  h <- .ensure_smoothed(); dates <- h$dates
  m <- nrow(kf_hat$vt)
   mats_raw <- if (exists("ranks") && length(ranks) == m) paste0(ranks, "m") else paste0(seq_len(m), "m")
  mats <- factor(mats_raw, levels = mats_raw)
  vt <- kf_hat$vt
  roll <- function(x, k) {
    n <- length(x); out <- rep(NA_real_, n)
    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      j0 <- max(1, i - k + 1); jj <- j0:i
      out[i] <- sqrt(mean(x[jj]^2, na.rm = TRUE))
    }
    out
  }
  df <- lapply(1:m, function(i) tibble(date = dates, maturity = mats[i], RMSE = roll(vt[i, ], window_weeks))) |>
    bind_rows()
  ggplot(df, aes(date, RMSE)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6, colour = "black") +
    facet_wrap(~ maturity, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(title = sprintf("Rolling %d-week RMSE of Innovations by Maturity", window_weeks),
         x = NULL, y = "RMSE (log units)") +
    theme_classic()
}

# --- A) Ensure filtered states exist (xf = kf_hat$att) ----------------------#
.ensure_filtered_states <- function() {
  stopifnot(exists("kf_hat"), is.matrix(kf_hat$att))
  T_len <- ncol(kf_hat$att)
  stopifnot(T_len > 0)

  # Dates: prefer obs_dates; fallback = colnames(Y); else integer index
  dates <- NULL
  if (exists("obs_dates")) {
    dates <- as.Date(obs_dates); dates <- tail(dates, T_len)
  } else if (exists("Y") && !is.null(colnames(Y))) {
    try_dates <- try(as.Date(colnames(Y)), silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(try_dates, "try-error") && !any(is.na(try_dates)))
      dates <- tail(try_dates, T_len)
  }
  if (is.null(dates)) dates <- seq_len(T_len)

  list(xf = kf_hat$att, dates = dates, T_len = T_len)
}

# --- B) Pickers (use FILTERED dates, not smoothed) --------------------------#
.pick_spaced_filt <- function(from, to, n = 6) {
  h <- .ensure_filtered_states(); dates <- h$dates
  if (!inherits(dates, "Date")) stop("Filtered picker needs real Date index (obs_dates or Date colnames(Y)).")

  from <- as.Date(from); to <- as.Date(to)
  idx <- which(dates >= from & dates <= to)
  if (!length(idx)) return(integer(0))
  if (length(idx) <= n) return(idx)
  unique(round(seq(min(idx), max(idx), length.out = n)))
}

.pick_mmdd_filt <- function(from, to, mm = 6, dd = 15, n_max = 6) {
  h <- .ensure_filtered_states(); dates <- h$dates
  if (!inherits(dates, "Date")) stop("Filtered picker needs real Date index (obs_dates or Date colnames(Y)).")

  from <- as.Date(from); to <- as.Date(to)
  yrs  <- intersect(unique(lubridate::year(dates)), lubridate::year(from):lubridate::year(to))
  idx  <- integer(0)

  for (yy in yrs) {
    target <- as.Date(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d", yy, mm, dd))
    cand   <- which(lubridate::year(dates) == yy)
    if (length(cand)) idx <- c(idx, cand[ which.min(abs(dates[cand] - target)) ])
  }
  if (length(idx) > n_max) idx <- unique(round(seq(min(idx), max(idx), length.out = n_max)))
  idx
}

# --- C) One overlay at t_idx using FILTERED states --------------------------#
.overlay_plot_idx_filt <- function(t_idx, in_levels = FALSE) {
  h <- .ensure_filtered_states()
  xf <- h$xf; dates <- h$dates; T_len <- h$T_len
  stopifnot(t_idx >= 1, t_idx <= T_len)

  m  <- if (exists("Y") && is.matrix(Y)) nrow(Y) else dim(ss_hat$Zt)[1]

  chi_t <- xf[1, t_idx]
  xi_t  <- xf[2, t_idx]

  Z_t <- ss_hat$Zt[, , t_idx]
  c_t <- ss_hat$ct[, t_idx]
  y_hat_log <- as.numeric(c_t + Z_t %*% c(chi_t, xi_t))
  y_obs_log <- as.numeric(Y[, t_idx])

  tau_pts <- if (exists("Tau") && is.matrix(Tau) && ncol(Tau) >= t_idx) Tau[, t_idx]
  else if (exists("ranks")) ranks/12 else seq_len(m)/12

  tau_grid <- seq(0, max(tau_pts, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 200)
  A_grid <- A_fun(
    T          = tau_grid,
    kappa      = theta_hat$kappa,
    mu_star    = theta_hat$mu_star,
    sigma_chi  = theta_hat$sigma_chi,
    sigma_xi   = theta_hat$sigma_xi,
    rho        = theta_hat$rho,
    lambda_chi = theta_hat$lambda_chi
  )
  y_grid_log <- A_grid + exp(-theta_hat$kappa * tau_grid) * chi_t + xi_t

  if (isTRUE(in_levels)) {
    y_obs  <- exp(y_obs_log); y_hat <- exp(y_hat_log); y_line <- exp(y_grid_log); ylab <- "Price (levels)"
  } else {
    y_obs  <- y_obs_log;      y_hat <- y_hat_log;      y_line <- y_grid_log;      ylab <- "log price"
  }

  df_pts  <- tibble::tibble(maturity_m = 12 * tau_pts, observed = y_obs, model = y_hat)
  df_line <- tibble::tibble(maturity_m = 12 * tau_grid, model = y_line)

  ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_line(data = df_line, ggplot2::aes(maturity_m, model),
                       colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(data = df_pts, ggplot2::aes(maturity_m, observed),
                        shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black",
                        size = 2.6, stroke = 0.9) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(data = df_pts, ggplot2::aes(maturity_m, model),
                        shape = 19, colour = "black", size = 1.8) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title = paste0(format(dates[t_idx], "%d %b %Y"), "  (Filtered states)"),
      x = "Maturity (months)", y = ylab
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 10)
}

# --- D) Print grid for FILTERED overlays -----------------------------------#
.print_grid_filt <- function(idx, title = NULL, ncol = 3, in_levels = FALSE, savepath = NULL) {
  plots <- lapply(idx, function(i) .overlay_plot_idx_filt(i, in_levels = in_levels))
  if (length(plots) == 0) stop("No plots to show for the chosen window.")
  grid <- cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = plots, ncol = ncol)
  fig  <- if (!is.null(title)) {
    top <- cowplot::ggdraw() + cowplot::draw_label(title, fontface = "bold", x = 0, hjust = 0)
    cowplot::plot_grid(top, grid, ncol = 1, rel_heights = c(0.08, 0.92))
  } else grid
  print(fig)
  if (!is.null(savepath)) {
    dir.create(dirname(savepath), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    ggplot2::ggsave(savepath, fig, width = 14,
                    height = max(6, ceiling(length(plots)/ncol)*2.2), dpi = 300)
  }
  invisible(fig)
}
```
